Problem 1.

Mostly empirical (see number 1991 --> not a physical law, unrealistic that laws of nature relate all these different inputs), also does not look like it is derived from a ODE, dynamic, closed-form (analytical), lumped (no space variation is described). This model is just a linear equation.

Problem 2.

Semi-mechanistic (could be based on rate laws, but rate constants would be from data), Remember empirical-to-mechanistic is a continuum, dynamic, but will evolve to steady state, numerical.

Problem 3.

Probably empirical, but hard to tell from information, probably closed-form (analytical), steady-state, distributed model (depends on space coordinates). In fact it is empirical, because the equation and dispersion parameters don't describe any physical law per se, but happen to fit observations. The dispersion parameters are actually fit to measurements in practice.

Problem 5.

While computing power is increasing it never really beats an analytical model if it is possible to find. One advantage of analytical models is you can understand the nature of the response (exactly how the dependent variable depends on time and other variables) just by looking at the equation. Also, when it comes to implementing a model, an analytical model will generally have less code, require fewer add-on packages, and run faster. However, if the model is complex or you want to extend it, going to a numerical model is probably easier.
